GAT1.short: Does shared interest strengthen the association between partner ratings and a yes?

UGM1.question: Do unexpected offers change responders’ feelings?
UGM1.short: Do unexpected offers change responders’ feelings?
UGM1.prediction: Offer gap and change from the previous offer both add to felt valence. Arousal rises with the size of surprises on either side.
UGM1.source: Heffner, Son and FeldmanHall, Study 1, [source study](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-021-01213-6). R48 permits publication of the aggregate comparisons from this publicly obtainable source.
UGM1.sample: Size counts contributing responders with within-person variation. Observations count fitted trials.
UGM1.method: Valence regressed on offer, difference from expectation and change from the preceding offer. Arousal fits use surprise magnitude separately by sign. Intervals resample whole players.
UGM1.basis: The gap and offer-change intervals include zero, and the negative-surprise arousal slope is unresolved.
UGM1.limit: Within-player associations cannot establish which feature of an offer caused a feeling.
UGM1.headline: Valence, expectation gap

CAD1.limit: Enjoyment stands in for interest. A speaker can appear in several resampled conversations.

ACC1.question: Does a change in reward trajectory predict first-play happiness?
ACC1.short: Does a change in reward trajectory predict first-play happiness?
ACC1.prediction: Prior work predicts a positive acceleration coefficient. The packet’s alternative forecast was an interval crossing zero. The positive reading requires all three fits to clear zero.
ACC1.source: Rutledge and colleagues, Great Brain Experiment first plays, Dryad (CC0). [Deposit](https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.prr4xgxkk).
ACC1.sample: The table identifies contributing people or paired observations for each estimate.
ACC1.method: Hold out whole players. Fit the second difference in realized reward on the test players under the frozen one-rate model, two-rate model and endpoint exclusion. Intervals resample whole test players.
ACC1.basis: All three held-out coefficients have positive lower bounds. The scale-end check and the two-rate fit retain the direction.
ACC1.limit: A rating comes every two or three trials. The last three rewards can reach before the previous rating. The preflight also found excess positive readings under a scale ceiling.
ACC1.headline: All players, one fading rate

ADP1.question: Do bad surprises fade more slowly than good surprises?
ADP1.short: Do bad surprises fade more slowly than good surprises?
ADP1.prediction: The curator predicts slower fading after bad surprises. The competing account predicts no difference by sign.
ADP1.source: Rutledge and colleagues, Great Brain Experiment first plays, Dryad (CC0). [Deposit](https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.prr4xgxkk).
ADP1.sample: The table identifies contributing people or paired observations for each estimate.
ADP1.method: Subtract the good-surprise fading rate from the bad-surprise rate. Larger rates retain more of an earlier surprise. Fit the fixed grid on held-out players and repeat after removing frequent scale-end users.
ADP1.basis: Both held-out intervals clear zero. Bad surprises retained more weight in the next few minutes of play.
ADP1.limit: A few minutes of a game is not a life. The rating scale has ends, and uncertainty is on the registered discrete grid.
ADP1.headline: All players, bad minus good fading rate

MNG1.question: Does caregiving lead daily activities in meaning relative to happiness?
MNG1.short: Does caregiving lead daily activities in meaning relative to happiness?

MNG1.source: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, ATUS Well-Being Module and Basic Activity/Who files, public-domain tables. [BLS module](https://www.bls.gov/tus/dictionaries.htm).
MNG1.sample: The table identifies contributing people or paired observations for each estimate.
MNG1.method: Subtract each respondent’s average rating on each scale, then compare the meaning and happiness departures. Weight the four years equally and resample whole people within year. Category intervals describe separate means.
MNG1.basis: Both care groups were above housework in point estimates, but paid work was above both. Volunteering had the largest activity estimate. Television had the lowest. Pairwise ranking intervals were not registered.
MNG1.limit: One word measures meaning. People select their activities and typically rate only three episodes. Early survey years had an activity-selection error, and the last wave omitted January and February.

MNG1.headline: child care

DRV1.question: Do accelerating falls in standing favor anxiety over sadness?
DRV1.short: Do accelerating falls in standing favor anxiety over sadness?
DRV1.prediction: A growing fall predicts high anxiety more strongly than high sadness. The all-pairs and short-gap readings must agree.
DRV1.source: Ryvkina status diaries, publicly available openESM members 0056 and 0057. R48 permits aggregate comparisons.
DRV1.sample: The table identifies contributing people or paired observations for each estimate.
DRV1.method: Within person, compare the two indicators while holding final standing and the size of the last fall. Short-gap fits cap both intervals at twice the diary median. Report thresholds and realized prevalence, including ties.
DRV1.basis: The full and short-gap readings establish no positive contrast. Anxiety was flagged in every report in both diaries. In 0056 the sadness indicator was also constant, so its exact zero cannot test the mechanism.
DRV1.limit: A second difference of noisy standing ratings is noisy. Only two diaries were available and missed prompts may be selective.
DRV1.withheld: All registered fits and clock checks are reported. A varying anxiety indicator is needed to distinguish the channels.
DRV1.headline: 0057, all, anxiety minus sadness
